```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(modelcompR))
t <- t_nounits
D <- D_nounits
```

A continuous model rarely lives alone. Balls bounce, doses are given at set
times, controllers sample a plant and update their outputs once per period,
and a simulation has to start from values that satisfy every algebraic
constraint of the model. This article covers the parts of modelcompR that
handle these situations:

1. symbolic events attached to a `System`, which correspond to the
   `continuous_events` and `discrete_events` of ModelingToolkit.jl;
2. the numeric callback layer that the solvers run, a port of the callbacks
   of DiffEqBase.jl and DiffEqCallbacks.jl;
3. clocks and synchronous discrete time systems, after the `Clock`,
   `Sample`, `Hold` and `ShiftIndex` operators of ModelingToolkit, including
   state machines;
4. initialization: initial conditions, bindings, guesses, `Initial(x)`,
   initialization equations, the initialization problem, and the
   `initializealg` options of the integrators.

# Symbolic continuous events

A continuous event has a *condition*, an equation `lhs ~ rhs` that becomes
true when `lhs - rhs` crosses zero, and an *affect*, a list of equations
that say how the state changes at that instant. The solver locates the
crossing by root finding on its dense interpolant, so the event time is
accurate to the tolerance of the root finder and not to the step size.

Affect equations relate the values after the event to the values before
it. `Pre(v)` is the value of `v` just before the event; a variable without
`Pre()` is the value after it. So `v ~ -Pre(v)` reverses the velocity.

## The bouncing ball

The classic example: a ball falls under gravity and bounces elastically
when it reaches the floor. The event is written as a pair
`list(conditions, affects)`.

```{r}
x <- Variable("x", t, default = 1)
v <- Variable("v", t, default = 0)
ball <- System(list(D(x) ~ v, D(v) ~ -9.8), t, name = "ball",
               continuous_events = list(list(x ~ 0), list(v ~ -Pre(v))))
continuous_events(ball)
ball <- mtkcompile(ball)
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(ball, list(), c(0, 3)), Tsit5())
sol$retcode
min(sol[x])
```

The times at which events fired are recorded in `sol$events`. For a drop
from height one the first impact is at `sqrt(2 / 9.8)`, and with an elastic
bounce every later impact comes two flight times after the previous one.

```{r}
ev_t <- vapply(sol$events, `[[`, 0, "t")
ev_t
sqrt(2 / 9.8) * c(1, 3, 5)
```

At each event time the solution keeps two rows, the state just before and
just after the affect, so the jump in the velocity is visible in the saved
values.

```{r}
i <- which(sol$t == ev_t[1])
sol[v][i]
plot(sol)
```

The constructor `SymbolicContinuousCallback()` builds the same event
explicitly, and `%=>%` is an infix shorthand for the pair. A condition list
with several equations fires when any of them crosses zero. Here a particle
moves between two walls at `y = -1.5` and `y = 1.5`:

```{r}
y <- Variable("y", t, default = 0)
vy <- Variable("vy", t, default = 2)
walls <- list(y ~ -1.5, y ~ 1.5) %=>% list(vy ~ -Pre(vy))
box <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(y) ~ vy, D(vy) ~ 0), t, name = "walls",
                         continuous_events = walls))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(box, list(), c(0, 4)))
vapply(sol$events, `[[`, 0, "t")
range(sol[y])
```

A list of single formulas, without affects, is a list of condition only
events. These only stop the integrator at the crossing, which is useful
to make the solver step exactly onto a discontinuity.

## Upward and downward crossings: `affect_neg`

By default an affect runs for crossings in both directions. `affect_neg`
gives a separate affect for downward crossings (where `lhs - rhs` goes from
positive to negative); `affect_neg = NULL` makes downward crossings stop the
integrator without changing anything. In the next example two counters
record how often `x = sin(t)` passes `0.5` upward and downward. Counters are
parameters, and a parameter may only be changed by an event when it is
declared in `discrete_parameters`; ModelingToolkit requires such parameters
to be time dependent, which is why they are created with `Parameter(name, t)`.

```{r}
x <- Variable("x", t, default = 0)
up <- Parameter("up", t, default = 0)
dn <- Parameter("dn", t, default = 0)
cross <- SymbolicContinuousCallback(list(x ~ 0.5), list(up ~ Pre(up) + 1),
                                    affect_neg = list(dn ~ Pre(dn) + 1),
                                    discrete_parameters = list(up, dn))
cs <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ cos(t)), t, name = "neg",
                        continuous_events = cross))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(cs, list(), c(0, 10)), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
c(up = sol$ps[up], down = sol$ps[dn])
vapply(sol$events, `[[`, 0, "t")
c(pi / 6, 5 * pi / 6, 13 * pi / 6, 17 * pi / 6)
```

`sol$ps[p]` gives the value of a parameter at the end of the solve. The
values in force at other times are kept as a parameter history, so the
solution can be indexed and interpolated in a discrete parameter just as in
an unknown.

The argument `rootfind` chooses where the affect is applied: `"left"` (the
default, SciMLBase's `LeftRootFind`) just before the crossing, `"right"`
just after it, and `"none"` at the end of the step that contains it.

# Symbolic discrete events

A discrete event is checked at specific times rather than located by root
finding. Its condition is one of:

* a number `dt`: a periodic event every `dt`;
* a numeric vector or a list of numbers: events at preset times (use
  `list(2)` for a single time, since a single number means a period);
* a `Clock()`: a periodic event with a phase, which also fires at the
  initial time when the clock ticks there;
* a symbolic boolean, which fires after a step when it holds.

## Preset times: a dose

A dose given at `t = 2` raises the input `d` of a first order decay. The
dose is a time dependent discrete parameter.

```{r}
yd <- Variable("yd", t, default = 1)
k <- Parameter("k", default = 1)
d <- Parameter("d", t, default = 0)
dose <- SymbolicDiscreteCallback(list(2), list(d ~ 1), discrete_parameters = d)
dsys <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(yd) ~ -k * yd + d), t, name = "dose",
                          discrete_events = dose))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(dsys, list(), c(0, 4)), Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
i <- which(sol$t == 2)
sol[d][i]
sol(c(1, 3), idxs = d)
c(tail(sol[yd], 1), 1 + (exp(-2) - 1) * exp(-2))
```

The rows before and after the event each carry the parameter values in
force with them, so `sol[d]` jumps from 0 to 1 exactly at `t = 2`. This
differs on purpose from ModelingToolkit 11, which gives both rows the
value after the event.

## Periodic events and `Discrete()` variables

`Discrete("c", t)` declares a discrete variable, the `@discretes` of
ModelingToolkit. It is stored as a parameter, and an affect equation with
it on the left-hand side changes it without listing it in
`discrete_parameters`. A period of `1.0` fires at `t = 1, 2, 3`:

```{r}
x <- Variable("x", t, default = 0)
cc <- Discrete("c", t, default = 1)
per <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ cc), t, name = "per",
                         discrete_events = list(1.0, list(cc ~ Pre(cc) + 1))))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(per, list(), c(0, 3.5)), reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-9)
c(sol$ps[cc], tail(sol[x], 1), 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 * 0.5)
```

A `Clock(dt, phase)` condition ticks on the absolute lattice
`phase + k dt`, including the initial time when it lies on the lattice, but
never at the final time.

```{r}
cnt <- Discrete("cnt", t, default = 0)
tick <- SymbolicDiscreteCallback(Clock(0.1), list(cnt ~ Pre(cnt) + 1))
clk <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ t), t, name = "clk", discrete_events = tick))
solve(ODEProblem(clk, list(x ~ 0, cnt ~ 0), c(0, 1)))$ps[cnt]
```

## Symbolic conditions

A condition can be a symbolic boolean built with symcompR's `Eq`, `<`, `&`
and so on. It is tested after every step, so pass the times it tests as
`tstops` to make the integrator step onto them. Here cells grow toward a
carrying level, and at `t = tinject` a batch of `M` cells is injected only
if the population is still below 50.

```{r}
N <- Variable("N", t, default = 0)
M <- Parameter("M", default = 50)
tinj <- Parameter("tinject", default = 10)
alpha <- Parameter("alpha", default = 100)
inject <- list(Eq(t, tinj), list(N ~ Pre(N) + M))
cells <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(N) ~ alpha - N), t, name = "cells",
                           discrete_events = inject))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(cells, list(), c(0, 20)), tstops = 10, reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-9)
sol[N][sol$t == 10]
guarded <- list(Eq(t, tinj) & (N < 50), list(N ~ Pre(N) + M))
cells2 <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(N) ~ alpha - N), t, name = "cells2",
                            discrete_events = guarded))
sol2 <- solve(ODEProblem(cells2, list(), c(0, 20)), tstops = 10, reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-9)
sum(sol2$t == 10)
```

The first model saves two rows at `t = 10` (before and after the
injection); in the second the guard is false and only one row is saved.
Note that `M` and `tinject`, used only in the event, are still parameters
of the compiled system.

# Kinds of affects

## Affects are solved with the model

Symbolic affects are not plain assignments. The affect equations are solved
together with the algebraic and observed equations of the system: unknowns
that the affect does not fix keep their values, and the others change so
that the system stays consistent. Setting the observed variable `y ~ 2x` to
3 therefore moves `x` to 1.5:

```{r}
x <- Variable("x", t, default = 1)
yo <- Variable("yo", t)
obs <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ 0, yo ~ 2 * x), t, name = "obs",
                         discrete_events = list(list(1), list(yo ~ 3))))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(obs, list(), c(0, 2)))
c(tail(sol[x], 1), tail(sol[yo], 1))
```

In a DAE with the constraint `x y = p`, incrementing `x` makes `y`
compensate. If instead `y` is held with `y ~ Pre(y)` and `p` is a discrete
parameter, the event changes `p`.

```{r}
x <- Variable("x", t, default = 1)
ya <- Variable("ya", t, guess = 1)
p <- Parameter("p", t, default = 2)
eqs <- list(x * ya ~ p, D(x) ~ 0)
s1 <- mtkcompile(System(eqs, t, name = "dae1",
                        discrete_events = list(list(1), list(x ~ Pre(x) + 1))))
sol1 <- solve(ODEProblem(s1, list(), c(0, 2)))
c(x = tail(sol1[x], 1), y = tail(sol1[ya], 1))
ev <- SymbolicDiscreteCallback(list(1), list(x ~ Pre(x) + 1, ya ~ Pre(ya)),
                               discrete_parameters = p)
s2 <- mtkcompile(System(eqs, t, name = "dae2", discrete_events = ev))
sol2 <- solve(ODEProblem(s2, list(), c(0, 2)))
c(y = tail(sol2[ya], 1), p = sol2$ps[p])
```

A parameter that is changed by an affect without being a discrete
parameter makes the affect unsolvable, and `solve()` reports it:

```{r}
dp <- Parameter("dp", default = 0)
nd <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ dp), t, name = "nd",
                        discrete_events = list(list(1), list(dp ~ 1))))
tryCatch(solve(ODEProblem(nd, list(), c(0, 2))), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

## `AssignmentAffect`

`AssignmentAffect()` assigns values computed entirely from the state
before the event: each right-hand side is wrapped in `Pre()`. A swap is
then simply written as two assignments.

```{r}
a <- Variable("a", t, default = 1)
b <- Variable("b", t, default = 2)
swap <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(a) ~ 0, D(b) ~ 0), t, name = "swap",
                          discrete_events = list(list(1),
                                                 AssignmentAffect(list(a ~ b, b ~ a)))))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(swap, list(), c(0, 2)))
c(tail(sol[a], 1), tail(sol[b], 1))
```

## Imperative affects

`ImperativeAffect(f, modified, observed, ctx)` runs an R function, the
functional or imperative affect of ModelingToolkit. `modified` and
`observed` are named lists of variables or expressions. When the event
fires, `f(modified, observed, ctx, integ)` receives their current values
as named lists and returns a named list of new values for some of the
`modified` entries. A furnace with hysteresis switches on below one
threshold and off above another:

```{r}
temp <- Variable("temp", t)
on_th <- Parameter("on_threshold", default = 0.5)
off_th <- Parameter("off_threshold", default = 0.7)
power <- Parameter("power", default = 1)
leak <- Parameter("leakage", default = 0.1)
on <- Discrete("furnace_on", t, default = 0)
off_ev <- SymbolicContinuousCallback(list(temp ~ off_th),
  ImperativeAffect(function(m, o, ctx, integ) list(furnace_on = 0),
                   modified = list(furnace_on = on)))
on_ev <- SymbolicContinuousCallback(list(temp ~ on_th),
  ImperativeAffect(function(m, o, ctx, integ) list(furnace_on = 1),
                   modified = list(on)))
heater <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(temp) ~ on * power - temp^2 * leak), t,
                            name = "heater", continuous_events = list(off_ev, on_ev)))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(heater, list(temp ~ 0, on ~ 1), c(0, 10)))
length(sol$events)
range(sol[temp][sol$t > sol$events[[1]]$t])
plot(sol)
```

Returning a name that is not in `modified` is an error ("Tried to write
back"), which catches typos. The `integ` argument is the integrator, so an
imperative affect can also stop the simulation with `terminate()`:

```{r}
x <- Variable("x", t, default = 0)
stop_at <- ImperativeAffect(function(m, o, ctx, integ) {
  terminate(integ)
  NULL
})
term <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ 1), t, name = "term",
                          continuous_events = list(list(x ~ 2), stop_at)))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(term, list(), c(0, 10)))
c(sol$retcode, tail(sol$t, 1))
```

## Initialize and finalize affects

An event may also carry affects that run once when the integration starts
(`initialize`) and once when it ends (`finalize`). The condition below never
fires; the event only sets `a` at the start and counts the finalization.

```{r}
a <- Parameter("a", t, default = 0)
b <- Parameter("b", t, default = 0)
life <- SymbolicContinuousCallback(list(x ~ 100), NULL, initialize = list(a ~ 3),
                                   finalize = list(b ~ Pre(b) + 1),
                                   discrete_parameters = list(a, b))
ls <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ a), t, name = "life", continuous_events = life))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(ls, list(), c(0, 1)))
c(a0 = sol[a][1], x1 = tail(sol[x], 1), b = sol$ps[b])
```

## Events of subsystems

Events of a subsystem are namespaced with it, so they keep working after
composition. `continuous_events()` collects the events of the whole
hierarchy, and `continuous_events_toplevel()` only those of the top system.

```{r}
xi <- Variable("xi", t, default = 1)
inner <- System(list(D(xi) ~ -1), t, name = "inner",
                continuous_events = list(list(xi ~ 0), list(xi ~ Pre(xi) + 1)))
outer <- System(list(), t, name = "outer", systems = list(inner))
continuous_events(outer)[[1]]$conditions[[1]]
length(continuous_events_toplevel(outer))
oc <- mtkcompile(outer)
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(oc, list(), c(0, 2.5)))
tail(sol[oc$inner$xi], 1)
```

# The numeric callback layer

Symbolic events compile to numeric callbacks, and the same callbacks can be
passed directly to `solve()` through `callback`, for problems built from R
functions as well as from systems. This is the interface of DiffEqBase.jl:
a condition is a function `(u, t, integ)` and an affect a function
`(integ)` that changes the integrator in place through `integ$u` and
`integ$p`.

## Continuous, discrete and vector callbacks

`ContinuousCallback(condition, affect)` fires when `condition` crosses
zero. The bouncing ball written with plain functions:

```{r}
fall <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(u[2], -9.8), c(1, 0), c(0, 2))
bounce <- ContinuousCallback(function(u, t, integ) u[1],
                             function(integ) integ$u[2] <- -integ$u[2])
sol <- solve(fall, Tsit5(), callback = bounce)
min(vapply(sol$u, `[`, 0, 1))
```

`VectorContinuousCallback()` takes a vector valued condition and calls
the affect with the index of the component that crossed. Two independent
balls dropped from different heights:

```{r}
two <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(u[3], u[4], -9.8, -9.8), c(1, 2, 0, 0), c(0, 2))
vcb <- VectorContinuousCallback(function(u, t, integ) u[1:2],
                                function(integ, idx) integ$u[idx + 2] <- -integ$u[idx + 2])
sol <- solve(two, Tsit5(), callback = vcb)
c(min(vapply(sol$u, `[`, 0, 1)), min(vapply(sol$u, `[`, 0, 2)))
```

`DiscreteCallback(condition, affect)` checks a logical condition after each
step. `PresetTimeCallback(times, affect)` fires at given times, which it
adds as stops of the integrator, and `PeriodicCallback(affect, dt)` fires
every `dt`. `CallbackSet()` combines any number of callbacks.

```{r}
decay <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) -u, 1, c(0, 3))
kick <- PresetTimeCallback(c(1, 2), function(integ) integ$u[1] <- integ$u[1] + 1)
hits <- 0
count <- PeriodicCallback(function(integ) hits <<- hits + 1, 0.5)
floor_cb <- DiscreteCallback(function(u, t, integ) u[1] < 0.2,
                             function(integ) integ$u[1] <- 0.2)
sol <- solve(decay, Tsit5(), callback = CallbackSet(kick, count, floor_cb))
hits
sol(c(0.99, 1.01, 2.5))
```

The periodic callback fired at `t = 0.5, 1, ..., 2.5`; it never fires at
the initial or final time unless `initial_affect` or `final_affect` asks
for it.

## Stopping and step control

`terminate(integ)` inside an affect stops the integration with retcode
`"Terminated"`. `TerminateSteadyState()` does this automatically when the
derivative falls below its tolerances, which is a convenient way to
integrate "until steady state":

```{r}
ss <- solve(ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) -u, 1, c(0, 1e6)), Tsit5(),
            callback = TerminateSteadyState())
c(ss$retcode, signif(tail(ss$t, 1), 4))
```

`StepsizeLimiter(dtFE)` caps the step at a fraction of a function of the
state, and `IterativeCallback(time_choice, affect)` schedules each next
event from the previous one.

```{r}
prob <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) -u, c(1, 2), c(0, 1))
max(diff(solve(prob, Tsit5(), callback = StepsizeLimiter(function(u, p, t) 0.01))$t))
times <- numeric()
it <- IterativeCallback(function(integ) if (integ$t < 0.7) integ$t + 0.3 else NULL,
                        function(integ) times <<- c(times, integ$t))
invisible(solve(prob, Tsit5(), callback = it))
times
```

## Saving and integrating

`SavingCallback(f, saved)` stores `f(u, t, integ)` in a `SavedValues()`
container at the times `saveat`, or after every step when `saveat` is
empty, without changing the steps of the solver.
`FunctionCallingCallback()` just calls a function.
`IntegratingSumCallback()` accumulates the integral of a function of the
state over the solve.

```{r}
sv <- SavedValues()
invisible(solve(prob, Tsit5(), callback = SavingCallback(function(u, t, integ) sum(u), sv,
                                                         saveat = 0.25)))
cbind(t = sv$t, saved = unlist(sv$saveval), exact = 3 * exp(-sv$t))
iv <- IntegrandValuesSum()
invisible(solve(prob, Tsit5(), callback = IntegratingSumCallback(function(u, t, integ) u, iv)))
rbind(callback = iv$integrand, exact = (1 - exp(-1)) * c(1, 2))
```

## Domains and manifolds

`PositiveDomain()` rejects steps that leave the positive orthant, and
`ManifoldProjection(g)` projects the state back onto the manifold
`g(u) = 0` after every step. With loose tolerances the harmonic oscillator
drifts off its circle; the projection keeps it there to rounding.

```{r}
ho <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(u[2], -u[1]), c(1, 0), c(0, 100))
free <- solve(ho, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-3, abstol = 1e-3)
proj <- solve(ho, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-3, abstol = 1e-3,
              callback = ManifoldProjection(function(u, p, t) sum(u^2) - 1))
c(free = sum(tail(free$u, 1)[[1]]^2) - 1, projected = sum(tail(proj$u, 1)[[1]]^2) - 1)
```

The other ports of DiffEqCallbacks.jl are `GeneralDomain()`,
`AutoAbstol()`, `IntegratingCallback()`, `IntegratingGKCallback()`,
`LinearizingSavingCallback()`, `ProbIntsUncertainty()` and
`AdaptiveProbIntsUncertainty()`; see their help pages.

# Clocks and synchronous systems

A clocked variable changes only at the ticks of a clock and holds its
value in between. modelcompR follows the synchronous semantics of
ModelingToolkit (after Modelica's chapter 16):

* `Clock(dt, phase)` is a periodic clock; `SolverStepClock()` ticks at
  every step of the solver; `ContinuousClock()` is the continuous time
  domain.
* `ShiftIndex(clock)` gives an index `k`: `k(x)` is `x` at the current tick
  and `(k - 1)(x)` the value one tick earlier. `Shift(t, -1)(x)` is the
  lower level operator.
* `Sample(clock)(x)` (or `Sample(x)`, with the clock inferred) reads a
  continuous variable at the ticks; `Hold(x)` turns a discrete variable into
  a piecewise constant continuous signal.

```{r}
xs <- Variable("xs", t)
kk <- ShiftIndex(Clock(0.1))
kk
(kk - 1)(xs)
shift2term(Shift(t, -2)(xs))
TimeDomain(kk(xs))
Clock(0.1, phase = 0.05)
```

## Pure discrete time systems

When every equation is a difference equation, `mtkcompile()` produces a
discrete time system that is solved as a `DiscreteProblem` with
`FunctionMap()`. The Fibonacci recursion needs the two past values:

```{r}
fy <- Variable("fy", t)
k <- ShiftIndex(t)
fib <- mtkcompile(System(list(fy ~ (k - 1)(fy) + (k - 2)(fy)), t, name = "fib"))
unknowns(fib)
sol <- solve(DiscreteProblem(fib, list((k - 1)(fy) ~ 1, (k - 2)(fy) ~ 0), c(0, 9)),
             FunctionMap())
sol[fy]
```

The unknowns are the delayed values; `fy` itself is observed. A value
given for `fy` instead of its past is taken as `fy` at the initial time,
and the past is solved for.

## A discrete controller on a continuous plant

The SampledData tutorial of ModelingToolkit closes a loop around a first
order plant with a discrete filter and a proportional controller, both on a
clock with period 0.5. The controller samples the plant output, and the
plant sees the held control signal.

```{r}
dt <- 0.5
k <- ShiftIndex(Clock(dt))
plant <- function(name) {
  x <- Variable("x", t, default = 1); u <- Variable("u", t); y <- Variable("y", t)
  System(list(D(x) ~ -x + u, y ~ x), t, name = name)
}
filt <- function(name) {
  x <- Variable("x", t, default = 0); u <- Variable("u", t, default = 0)
  y <- Variable("y", t, default = 0)
  a <- 1 / exp(dt)
  System(list(k(x) ~ a * (k - 1)(x) + (1 - a) * k(u), y ~ x), t, name = name)
}
controller <- function(kp, name) {
  y <- Variable("y", t); r <- Variable("r", t, default = 0)
  ud <- Variable("ud", t, default = 0); yd <- Variable("yd", t, default = 0)
  kpp <- Parameter("kp", default = kp)
  System(list(yd ~ Sample(y), ud ~ kpp * (r - yd)), t, name = name)
}
r <- Variable("r", t)
f <- filt("f"); c1 <- controller(1, "c"); p1 <- plant("p")
conns <- list(r ~ sin(t), f$u ~ r, f$y ~ c1$r, Hold(c1$ud) ~ p1$u, p1$y ~ c1$y)
cl <- mtkcompile(System(conns, t, systems = list(f, c1, p1), name = "cl"))
unknowns(cl)
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(cl, list(), c(0, 5)), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-12)
sol(seq(0.25, 2.25, by = dt), idxs = cl$c$ud)
plot(sol)
```

Clock inference partitions the equations: the plant stays continuous and
its state is the only unknown (printed as its alias `c₊y`, the controller
input connected to it), while the filter and controller variables
become discrete parameters updated by a periodic callback at the ticks.
`sol(t, idxs = cl$c$ud)` is piecewise constant. Inconsistent clocks, such
as a difference equation on a continuous variable or two different clocks
in one partition, are rejected by `mtkcompile()`.

A variable indexed with a zero shift takes the clock of the index, so
`k(y) ~ -Sample(x)` samples `x` on that clock:

```{r}
xc <- Variable("xc", t); yc <- Variable("yc", t)
k2 <- ShiftIndex(Clock(0.5))
sm <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(xc) ~ -xc + Hold(yc), k2(yc) ~ -Sample(xc)), t, name = "sampled"))
so <- solve(ODEProblem(sm, list(xc ~ 1, yc ~ 0), c(0, 1)), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-12)
c(so(c(0.25, 0.75), idxs = yc), -1, 1 - 2 * exp(-0.5))
```

## Ticking with the solver: `SolverStepClock`

`SolverStepClock()` ticks at the initial time and after every accepted
step of the integrator, so a discrete variable on it counts steps. Each
tick saves the rows before and after the update, so the distinct times are
counted.

```{r}
xn <- Variable("xn", t, default = 1)
nstep <- Variable("nstep", t, default = 0)
ks <- ShiftIndex(SolverStepClock())
stepper <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(xn) ~ -xn, ks(nstep) ~ (ks - 1)(nstep) + 1), t,
                             name = "stepper"))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(stepper, list(), c(0, 1)), Tsit5())
c(steps = length(unique(sol$t)) - 1, counter = sol$ps[stepper$nstep])
```

## State machines

A state machine is a set of states, each a system of clocked equations,
with `initial_state(s)` and `transition(from, to, cond)` equations between
them. Inside states and conditions, `ticksInState()`, `timeInState()`,
`entry()` and `activeState(s)` refer to the time spent in a state.
ModelingToolkit 11 extracts state machines but cannot simulate them;
modelcompR compiles each machine into a periodic callback with the
semantics of Modelica's chapter 17. This is an extension. The machine
below counts up for three ticks and down for two.

```{r}
k <- ShiftIndex(Clock(1))
xm <- GlobalScope(Variable("xm", t, default = 0))
up_s <- System(list(k(xm) ~ (k - 1)(xm) + 1), t, list(xm), list(), name = "up")
down_s <- System(list(k(xm) ~ (k - 1)(xm) - 1), t, list(xm), list(), name = "down")
machine <- System(list(initial_state(up_s),
                       transition(up_s, down_s, ticksInState() >= 3, immediate = FALSE, reset = FALSE),
                       transition(down_s, up_s, ticksInState() >= 2, immediate = FALSE, reset = FALSE)),
                  t, systems = list(up_s, down_s), name = "sm")
equations(machine)[[2]]
z <- Variable("z", t, default = 0)
mm <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(z) ~ Hold(xm)), t, systems = list(machine), name = "smodel"))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(mm, list(), c(0, 10)))
unname(sol(seq(0.5, 9.5, by = 1), idxs = xm))
```

With `immediate = TRUE` (the default) a transition fires at the tick where
its condition holds, before the equations of the source state run, and
`reset = TRUE` restarts the target state from the start values of its
variables. Hierarchical machines and `synchronize = TRUE` are not
supported.

# Initialization

Before an integrator can take its first step, the initial values must be
consistent: every algebraic equation must hold, derivative conditions must
be met, and parameters that are defined implicitly must be solved for. For
an ODE where every unknown has a value this is trivial; for a DAE it is a
nonlinear problem in its own right. modelcompR builds that problem
symbolically, as ModelingToolkit does.

## Initial conditions, bindings and guesses

Three kinds of values take part:

* **initial conditions** fix a value at the initial time: the `default` of
  a variable, or an entry of the operating point passed to `ODEProblem()`
  (`x ~ 0.6`). They become equations of the initialization system.
* **bindings** define a parameter as an expression of other quantities, for
  example `bindings = list(r ~ Initial(z))`; a parameter bound to `NA` is
  solved for.
* **guesses** are only starting points of the nonlinear solver. They do not
  constrain the result, but they choose the root when there are several.

The unit circle DAE `x' = -x + y`, `0 = x^2 + y^2 - 1` makes the
difference visible: fixing `x = 0.6` leaves two consistent values of `y`,
and the guess chooses between them.

```{r}
cx <- Variable("cx", t); cy <- Variable("cy", t)
circle <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(cx) ~ -cx + cy, 0 ~ cx^2 + cy^2 - 1), t, name = "circle"))
p_up <- ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6), c(0, 1), guesses = list(cy ~ 1))
p_dn <- ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6), c(0, 1), guesses = list(cy ~ -1))
c(up = p_up[cy], down = p_dn[cy])
p_up$initialization_data$retcode
```

Guesses can also be given on a variable, `Variable("y", t, guess = 1)`, or
on a system, `System(..., guesses = list(...))`; `guesses(sys)` and
`hasguess()` / `getguess()` inspect them.

## Missing guesses

When an unknown of the initialization system has neither a value nor a
guess, `missing_guess_value` decides what happens. The default is a
reproducible pseudo random start in `[0, 1)`;
`MissingGuessValue$Constant(v)` starts from `v`, and
`MissingGuessValue$Error()` stops with an error naming the variables.

```{r}
c(ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6), c(0, 1),
             missing_guess_value = MissingGuessValue$Constant(0.5))[cy],
  ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6), c(0, 1),
             missing_guess_value = MissingGuessValue$Constant(-0.5))[cy])
tryCatch(ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6), c(0, 1),
                    missing_guess_value = MissingGuessValue$Error()),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

## Derivatives and observed variables as conditions

Initial conditions are not limited to unknowns. A Lotka Volterra model can
be started at its steady state by setting both derivatives to zero, or
constrained through an observed variable.

```{r}
xl <- Variable("xl", t); yl <- Variable("yl", t); zl <- Variable("zl", t)
al <- Parameter("al", default = 1.5); be <- Parameter("be", default = 1)
ga <- Parameter("ga", default = 3); de <- Parameter("de", default = 1)
lv <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(xl) ~ al * xl - be * xl * yl,
                             D(yl) ~ -ga * yl + de * xl * yl, zl ~ xl + yl), t, name = "lv"))
steady <- ODEProblem(lv, list(D(xl) ~ 0, D(yl) ~ 0), c(0, 10), guesses = list(xl ~ 2.5, yl ~ 2))
c(steady[xl], steady[yl])
obs_ic <- ODEProblem(lv, list(D(xl) ~ 0, zl ~ 2), c(0, 10), guesses = list(xl ~ 1, yl ~ 1))
c(obs_ic[xl], obs_ic[yl])
```

Initial conditions may also be expressions of parameters, such as
`xl ~ 2 * al`.

## Initialization equations

Extra equations that hold only at the initial time are given as
`initialization_eqs`, either to the problem or to the system.

```{r}
xe <- Variable("xe", t); ye <- Variable("ye", t)
ie <- list(D(xe) ~ -xe * ye, D(ye) ~ xe - ye)
s_ie <- mtkcompile(System(ie, t, name = "ie"))
pr <- ODEProblem(s_ie, list(xe ~ 3), c(0, 1), guesses = list(ye ~ 1),
                 initialization_eqs = list(xe^2 + ye^2 ~ 25))
c(pr[xe], pr[ye])
s_ie2 <- mtkcompile(System(ie, t, name = "ie2", initialization_eqs = list(xe + ye ~ 5)))
pr2 <- ODEProblem(s_ie2, list(xe ~ 1), c(0, 1), guesses = list(ye ~ 1))
c(pr2[xe], pr2[ye])
```

## Parameters solved by initialization

A parameter with `default = NA` and an equation that determines it is an
unknown of the initialization system. Here `total ~ x + y` defines
`total` from the initial state:

```{r}
xp <- Variable("xp", t); yp <- Variable("yp", t)
total <- Parameter("total", default = NA)
ps <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(xp) ~ -xp, total ~ xp + yp), t, name = "paraminit"))
pp <- ODEProblem(ps, list(xp ~ 1, yp ~ 2), c(0, 1))
pp$ps[total]
```

To go the other way, solving for `xp` given `total`, the value of `xp`
must be removed (with `list(xp, NULL)`), otherwise the conditions
contradict each other:

```{r}
pp2 <- remake(pp, u0 = list(yp ~ 1, list(xp, NULL)), p = list(total ~ 4))
c(pp2[xp], pp2$ps[total])
```

## `Initial(x)`

`Initial(x)` is a parameter holding the initial value of `x`. Each
condition `x ~ 0.6` becomes the equation `x ~ Initial(x)` of the
initialization system, with the number stored in the parameter, so a new
value does not require a new initialization system. A binding can also
refer to it: below `r` is bound to the initial value of the algebraic
variable `z`, which solves `z^3 + z = x`.

```{r}
xi <- Variable("xi", t); zi <- Variable("zi", t); r <- Parameter("r")
ib <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(xi) ~ -r * xi, 0 ~ zi^3 + zi - xi), t, name = "ib",
                        bindings = list(r ~ Initial(zi)), guesses = list(zi ~ 1)))
parameters(ib)
Filter(isinitial, parameters(ib, initial_parameters = TRUE))
pi1 <- ODEProblem(ib, list(xi ~ 2), c(0, 1))
c(z = pi1[zi], r = pi1$ps[r], Initial_z = pi1$ps[Initial(zi)])
c(r_after_remake = remake(pi1, u0 = list(xi ~ 10))$ps[r])
```

Setting an `Initial` parameter of a problem in place runs initialization
again:

```{r}
pi1$ps[Initial(xi)] <- 10
c(pi1[xi], pi1[zi], pi1$ps[r])
```

## Over and underdetermined initialization

The initialization system is square only when the conditions exactly
determine the state. With fewer conditions it is underdetermined and
solved in the least squares sense from the guesses; with more it is
overdetermined and solved as a least squares problem, which succeeds when
the extra conditions are consistent and fails otherwise. Both cases warn,
and `fully_determined = TRUE` turns the warning into an error.

```{r}
under <- withCallingHandlers(
  ODEProblem(circle, list(), c(0, 1), guesses = list(cx ~ 0.5, cy ~ 1)),
  warning = function(w) { message("warning: ", conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
sum(under$u0^2)
tryCatch(ODEProblem(circle, list(), c(0, 1), guesses = list(cx ~ 0.5, cy ~ 1),
                    fully_determined = TRUE),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

Values for every unknown that already satisfy the constraint are kept
as they are; contradictory ones produce an
`InitializationFailure`, whose `solve()` returns retcode
`"InitialFailure"` at once.

```{r}
ok <- ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6, cy ~ 0.8), c(0, 1))
unname(ok$u0)
bad <- suppressWarnings(ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6, cy ~ 0.5), c(0, 1)))
class(bad)[1]
solve(bad)$retcode
```

`warn_initialize_determined = FALSE` silences the warnings, and
`check_initialization = FALSE` skips initialization altogether, taking the
values as given. `analyze_initialization_jacobian()` explains an
underdetermined system through the rank of its Jacobian and lists the free
unknowns.

```{r}
iu <- suppressWarnings(InitializationProblem(circle, 0, list(),
                                             guesses = list(cx ~ 0.5, cy ~ 1)))
res <- analyze_initialization_jacobian(iu, verbose = FALSE)
c(rank = res$rank, nullity = res$nullity, redundancy = res$redundancy)
```

## The initialization system and problem

`generate_initializesystem()` returns the symbolic initialization system,
and `InitializationProblem()` the numeric problem that `ODEProblem()`
solves internally. Its type follows ModelingToolkit: a `LinearProblem` for
an affine system, an `SCCNonlinearProblem` (solved block by block) for a
square nonlinear one, a `NonlinearProblem` with `use_scc = FALSE`, and a
`NonlinearLeastSquaresProblem` when the system is not square.

```{r}
isys <- generate_initializesystem(circle, op = list(cx ~ 0.6), guesses = list(cy ~ 1))
unknowns(isys)
equations(isys)
iprob <- InitializationProblem(circle, 0, list(cx ~ 0.6), guesses = list(cy ~ 1))
class(iprob)[1]
isol <- solve(iprob)
c(isol[cx], isol[cy])
class(p_up$initialization_data$initializeprob)[1]
```

`initialization_equations(sys)`, `get_initialization_eqs()`,
`initial_conditions()` and `guesses()` inspect the pieces of a system, and
`has_initialization_data()` tells whether a problem carries an
initialization problem. An ODE whose unknowns all have values needs none:

```{r}
xo <- Variable("xo", t); ko <- Parameter("ko", default = 2)
plain <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(xo) ~ -ko * xo), t, name = "plain"))
is.null(ODEProblem(plain, list(xo ~ 1), c(0, 1))$initialization_data)
```

## Reinitialization after `remake`

`remake()` runs initialization again with the new values. When only the
numbers change, the compiled initialization system is reused.

```{r}
p2 <- remake(p_up, u0 = list(cx ~ 0.8))
c(p2[cx], p2[cy])
s2 <- remake(obs_ic, u0 = list(zl ~ 3))
identical(s2$initialization_data$signature, obs_ic$initialization_data$signature)
c(s2[xl], s2[yl])
```

A numeric `u0` is taken as conditions on the differential variables and
as new starting values of the algebraic ones; `check_initialization = FALSE`
keeps the values exactly as given.

```{r}
unname(remake(p_up, u0 = c(0, 0.5))$u0)
unname(remake(p_up, u0 = c(0.1, 0.2), check_initialization = FALSE)$u0)
```

## The `initializealg` options of the integrators

Independently of the symbolic initialization, the DAE integrators can make
the initial values consistent themselves. `solve(prob, alg, initializealg =
...)` accepts the algorithms of OrdinaryDiffEq:

* `BrownFullBasicInit()` keeps the differential variables and solves the
  algebraic equations for the algebraic ones;
* `ShampineCollocationInit()` takes a small implicit Euler step to find
  consistent values of all variables;
* `CheckInit()` only checks the residual and fails with
  `"InitialFailure"`;
* `NoInit()` takes the values as they are;
* `OverrideInit()` solves the problem's initialization problem, and
  `DefaultInit()` uses `OverrideInit()` when there is one and `CheckInit()`
  otherwise.

Start the circle DAE from an inconsistent point without symbolic
initialization and let the integrator repair it:

```{r}
raw <- ODEProblem(circle, list(cx ~ 0.6, cy ~ 0.5), c(0, 1), check_initialization = FALSE)
fixed <- solve(raw, Rodas5P(), initializealg = BrownFullBasicInit())
c(fixed$retcode, round(fixed[cy][1], 6))
solve(raw, Rodas5P(), initializealg = CheckInit())$retcode
```

`CheckInit()` warns and returns `"InitialFailure"` because the constraint
does not hold at the given point.

The same algorithms apply to fully implicit `DAEProblem`s built from R
functions:

```{r}
fi <- function(du, u, p, t) c(du[1] + u[1], u[2] - 2 * u[1])
dprob <- DAEProblem(fi, c(0, 0), c(1, 5), c(0, 1), differential_vars = c(TRUE, FALSE))
solve(dprob, DFBDF(), initializealg = BrownFullBasicInit())$u[[1]]
```

After an event that changes the state of a DAE, the solver makes the
algebraic values consistent again in the same way; symbolic affects are
consistent by construction, which is why the `reinitializealg` argument of
the symbolic callbacks is kept only for compatibility.
